headline: Washington seeks more time in Supreme Court cannabis residency case
dek: Washington wants until 19 January 2027 to answer Peridot Tree's petition; the challengers say the delay would push any hearing on residency rules to next term.
key_points: Washington's attorney general asked the US Supreme Court on 13 November for a second extension, moving its response deadline in Peridot Tree v. Washington from 4 December to 19 January 2027.
Peridot Tree, owned by a Michigan resident denied a Washington dispensary licence, opposed the request the same day.
The case asks whether the Constitution's dormant Commerce Clause bars states and cities from favouring residents in cannabis licensing; federal appeals courts are split.
If the extension is granted, the challengers say the case would likely not be argued until autumn 2027 even if the justices take it.
body: Washington state has asked the US Supreme Court for more time, again, in the case that could decide whether states may reserve cannabis licences for their own residents. In a letter filed on 13 November, the Washington Liquor and Cannabis Board asked to move its deadline to respond to Peridot Tree's petition from 4 December to 19 January 2027, an extra 46 days on top of the 50 the court granted in October.

The challengers objected the same day. Their lawyer told the court the question is being litigated in many courts and that a longer delay would leave virtually no chance of the case being heard before the summer recess if the justices agree to take it. The court has not yet ruled on the request.

Peridot Tree WA is majority-owned by Kenneth Gay, a Michigan resident. Washington requires anyone applying to own a dispensary to have lived in the state for at least six months, and it rejected the company's application because of Gay's residency, according to the petition. A sister company, Peridot Tree Inc., was shut out of Sacramento licences reserved for current or former city residents. The two cases were combined on appeal.

In January the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld both the Washington and Sacramento rules. It reasoned that the dormant Commerce Clause, the constitutional principle that stops states discriminating against out-of-state commerce, does not need to protect a market that federal law prohibits. The full Ninth Circuit declined to rehear the case on 13 April, and Justice Elena Kagan gave the challengers until 10 September to file their petition, the Supreme Court docket shows.
## A split the court is asked to settle

The Ninth Circuit's view conflicts with two other appeals courts. The First Circuit struck down Maine's residency rule for medical cannabis businesses in 2022, and the Second Circuit ruled in August 2025 that New York's licensing priority for people with New York cannabis convictions was unconstitutional, as Cannabis Business Times has reported. That leaves states in the First and Second Circuits bound by one rule and the nine states of the Ninth Circuit, including California, Washington and Oregon, bound by the opposite one.

Circuit splits are one of the main reasons the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case. The petition asks the justices to decide whether state and city cannabis licensing schemes are subject to the Constitution's nondiscrimination principle at all.
> Every month this case waits is another month of residency rules that are legal in Seattle and unconstitutional in Portland, Maine.

Washington's deputy solicitor general, Tera Heintz, cited the workload of the state's small Supreme Court team in its first request on 2 October, including several other briefs and a merits brief due in October. The Marijuana Herald reported that the second request makes a similar case and argues the justices would still have time to decide whether to hear the case before the term ends in June. The City of Sacramento does not oppose the new extension, the Herald reported.

The challengers' reply turns on the calendar. Under the current schedule, Washington's brief is due 4 December and their reply 14 December, which they say leaves a reasonable chance of argument this term if review is granted. Under Washington's schedule, they argue, the case would likely not be heard until next autumn. They also noted that when they asked for a 60-day extension to file their petition, Washington agreed to only 30 days.
By MetaFlora's count, if the court grants the new request, Washington will have had 96 extra days to respond, and the state's brief would land more than four months after the petition was filed.
## What is at stake for operators

Residency rules and local-preference licensing are common in state cannabis markets, often as a way to keep licences out of the hands of large out-of-state companies or to reward communities harmed by enforcement. A Supreme Court ruling that the dormant Commerce Clause applies would expose many of those rules to challenge and open licensing rounds to out-of-state owners. A ruling the other way would let states keep them, at least while marijuana remains federally illegal.

Rescheduling adds a wrinkle. The Ninth Circuit's reasoning rests on federal prohibition. Medical marijuana under a state licence is now in Schedule III, though adult-use marijuana remains in Schedule I, so the question of what Congress has and has not prohibited is shifting under the case.

The clerk's office usually acts quickly on extension requests, so a decision could come within days. If it is denied, Washington's brief is due on 4 December and the challengers' reply on 14 December, and the petition could reach a conference early in 2027. If it is granted, the new deadline is 19 January 2027. Watch also for amicus briefs from states and industry groups, a sign of how much weight the court is being asked to give the issue.
